BY OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS: ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD AND ON THE CROSS. (In passionem et crucem Domini.)

1. “And when they came to a place called Golgotha, which is called the Place of the Skull, they gave him wine to drink mixed with gall. And when he had tasted it, he would not drink. And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. And sitting down, they kept watch over him there,” and so on. The passage just read is from the Gospel. To make it clear, it is good to have recourse to the saints and to receive its meaning from them, for it is more fitting for them than for us to stand as witnesses to the Gospels. And so that we do not drag out our discourse by going round all of them, the Apostle alone is enough to be our teacher and give us full assurance. For the blessed Paul himself writes to the Hebrews [?]

that it is impossible for God to lie; and he speaks most truly in saying it, and does not lie. For created things have it as a property of their nature to change and to be moved by all kinds of alterations, since, not having existed at one time, they underwent a change into being by the grace and love for humankind of the one who made them. As Paul says again: “Who calls the things that are not as though they were.” But God, who is the maker of all things through the Word and who truly is, has together with the Word a nature that cannot change. He teaches this through the prophet, saying: “See, see that I am, and I have not changed.” Therefore it is sung in the Psalms concerning men: “I said in my alarm, Every man is a liar”; but concerning God, Moses testifies in the law that “God is faithful and true.” 2. So the Christ-bearing man, as one taught by both of these, and himself explaining how God differs from created things, writes: “But let God be [?]

[?] …did not tell the truth, but acted lawlessly against the one who had given him, contriving death for the Lord in return for grace. They were therefore rightly cast off, and the death which they brought upon the Lord by lying, they truly drew down upon themselves. So too with Ananias and Sapphira in the Acts of the Apostles: having made a promise to God, they kept back part of what they had promised. They escaped the notice of everyone else, but Peter, the minister of the truth, thrust them away, saying: “You have not lied to men, but to God.” And in this a very great wonder took place, for what Peter alone knew he made plain to all through the death of Ananias, so that everyone came to reverence and feared the example of Sapphira. 3. For we must know and not be ignorant that what we promise to God is no longer ours, but belongs to God. And if we withdraw anything from it, we are not like people taking what is their own, but like people committing sacrilege by robbing what is God's. And the promise reaches not only as far as [?]

money, but extends even to speech and to the will itself. For if someone is poor in money, he is not also poor in will. Indeed, our great and truly divine mystery no longer has its pledge in money, but in a perfect will and in faith toward God. So we have all made promises, and we are all debtors of a promise. It is therefore necessary for the virgin to render virginity, such as she promised; for the continent, continence; for those in marriage, chastity and love and honor toward one another; and finally for all, faith toward God, and reverence, and righteousness, and courage, so that the example of Ananias and Sapphira may not overtake us as ungrateful people. For this reason the apostolic word also secures us beforehand: “Render to all what is due: tribute to whom tribute is due, honor to whom honor is due. Owe no one anything except to love one another.” The one who proclaimed these things did this himself. That is why he speaks boldly when he writes: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; from now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the righteous judge will award me.” For since he did not lie in what he promised but kept his pledge to God, he in turn received the promise from the true God without fail. 4. This, then, is why he counsels us, saying: “Do not lie to one another”; and again: “Let no falsehood come out of your mouth.” For he wants us to become imitators of himself, writing: “I speak the truth, I do not lie.” It is also a saying of the Lord in the Gospel that our Yes should be yes and our No, no. Let those who are in Christ confirm their words up to this point, and let us not go further and take refuge in oaths, so as to swear by God even for the sake of perishable money, especially since Moses lays down the law: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.” For if someone is worthy at all to name God, he is trustworthy enough to be believed even without an oath; for one who has become fit for the greater thing would be much more fit for the lesser. But if he is not trustworthy enough to be believed without an oath, then he is not worthy even to name the name of the Lord; he is not faithful in word. For how could God bear witness at all for such a man when he swears, since he has no faith, which is what the Lord looks to? Wisdom is witness to this when she says: “For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from foolish thoughts, and will not dwell [?]

in a body enslaved to sins.” For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ also first demands faith from those who call on him. He says in the case of the blind man: “Do you believe that I am able to do this for you?” and in the case of the epileptic: “If you believe, it is done.” The Savior demands this, not because he needed help from others, for he himself is the Lord and giver of faith, but so that he would not seem to show favor to persons, but rather to grant his assent to those who believe; and also so that they would not receive his benefits without faith and then lose them through unbelief. For when he gives grace, he wants the grace to remain, and when he heals, he wants the healing to last. So he safeguarded the paralytic, saying: “See, you have been made well; sin no more, so that nothing worse may happen to you.” A physician going in to the sick would first ask whether they wish to be treated, so that his treatment does not prove useless through their unwillingness while he takes pains, with the sick resisting the physician's art. In the same way the Lord questioned those who were being healed and granted grace to those who believed, so that by faith they might be able to hold fast to the grace. For faith is a sign of the soul's will. 5. Why, then, do those who have no faith in truth call God as witness? The Spirit testifies in the Psalms: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth,” and only through truth can God be called upon. So why do those who do not have faith even in small things swear by God? Besides, an oath is a witness to truth, not a statement about the facts. For people swear, not in order to state the facts, but to vouch for the truth and to show that they are not lying in what they say. If, then, the one who swears has faith and truth, what need is there of the oath? But if there is no faith in him, why do we act so impiously as to call God, who is above man, as witness for human and mortal matters? If it is not lawful to call even the earthly king as a witness in the outside courts, since he is higher than both the accusers and the judges, why do we call the Unbegotten into the affairs of begotten things and cause God to be despised by men? Away with it! This exceeds every lawlessness and audacity. What, then, must we do? Nothing more than let our Yes be yes and our No, no, and not lie at all. For in this way, by telling the truth, we would be seen to imitate the true God in this too. 6. But perhaps someone might reasonably object to this, saying: “If the oath has been forbidden to men, and by not swearing a person imitates the Divine, how is God himself said to swear in the divine Scriptures? For he swore to Abraham, as Moses also testifies, [?]

and it is written in the Hymns: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’ These passages will seem either to contradict what was said before, or to incite men to oaths.” But it is not so; let no one think this. For God swears by nothing. How could he, since he himself is the Lord and maker of all things? If one must speak the truth, his word is his oath. It gives full assurance to those who hear it and provides faith to each that what he has promised and speaks will certainly come to pass. For God does not swear as a man does; rather, his word serves us as an oath for the truth. He is said to swear when speaking to men, and this is because the saints speak in a more human fashion, so that from the very way they themselves are accustomed to speak, they may believe God when he speaks. For just as an oath confirms the word of men, so let what God says be reckoned as an oath, because of the firmness and unchangeableness of his counsel. The written oath itself bears witness to what is said: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent,” since an oath is something not to be repented of and certain to come to pass according to the promise. God himself also indicates this in Genesis, saying: “By myself I have sworn.” But this is not an oath. For he did not swear by someone else, which is the mark of an oath, but by himself, which escapes the notion of an oath; and by this he signifies the firmness of the promise and that the hearer must certainly believe. Let the hymn-writer also be a witness to what is said, as he reminds God, singing and saying: “Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?” For God does not swear by the truth; rather, what he speaks truthfully serves men as an oath to bring them to faith. So neither does God swear as men do, nor ought we to be incited to oaths by these passages. Rather, let us say and do such things that those who hear us do not need an oath, but our words carry in themselves the testimony of truth. In this way we shall truly imitate the Divine. 7. But perhaps someone might also ask about the Ninevites in this way: “If God's word is his oath, because in speaking he tells the truth and does not lie, how is it that when he said, ‘Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown,’ he did not fulfill the word?” For this too will seem to conflict with what was said at first. But God does not lie, God forbid! Nor did his word remain unfulfilled. For by his love for humankind he blunted his anger, and [?]

he looked to the repentance of the Ninevites rather than to their earlier sin. And the word of God did not mean that Nineveh would be razed after three days, but “I will bear with you for three days,” so that during the forbearance of three days they might have the power to repent, or else to choose the wrath that would follow. For what does the prophet say? “Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” He did not say, “After three days it will be overthrown,” for if he had, it would certainly have happened; but “Yet three days, and it will be overthrown,” so that in the word “yet” we might understand God's forbearance, and in the overthrow the wrath that would come after the forbearance if they did not repent. Otherwise, if it were not so, and he had not put off the three days for the sake of men's repentance, what prevented God from destroying them at once [?]? Weakness? Away with it! May this never even enter our mind. For God is the Lord of hosts, strong and mighty. Ignorance, then, of those people's deeds? Let not this be said either, for he knows all things before they come to be. What remains to understand, then, except the patience and love for humankind of the Master? The prophet knew this. That is why he fled at first when he was sent, and the second time, defending himself, he says: “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I hastened to flee to Tarshish, because I knew that you are merciful and compassionate, patient and abounding in mercy, and that you relent from evil.” Jonah fled, not to oppose God; and he grieved, not because he would have rejoiced at the destruction of the Ninevites. He did this out of care for the Ninevites. For he was afraid that they would think him unreliable, and that from then on they would no longer believe prophets, and the prophetic word would lose its credit among them. This is also why he lost heart [?]: so that he might be corrected by the Master, and it might become plain to all the Ninevites there that they were pardoned, not because the prophet had lied, but because of God's love for humankind. For he knew the patience signified by the word “yet.” And this is the custom of divine Scripture: when God wishes to signify his own patience, he announces it through the word “yet.” So he says through Isaiah: “What more shall I yet do for my vineyard that I have not done?” and through Jeremiah: “Therefore I will yet contend with you, says the Lord.” By saying “yet” he shows his [?]

goodness and forbearance. For he says: “Pass over to the islands of Kittim, and send to Kedar [?], and see.” If he had not wished to be patient, he would not have given them exhortations to pass over and, having passed over, to learn from opposites how they compare with what is good. Indeed, when a person's conduct no longer calls for patience but for wrath, then he declares: “I will no longer bear your sins.” And by the word “no longer” used here, he clearly shows the patience indicated by “yet” in the case of the Ninevites, and the truth of his word. For it was impossible for God not to be truthful when he speaks, or even when he merely wills. This is why, when he made a promise to Abraham, he did not lie, but granted him the son; and he brought the people out of Egypt through Moses the hierophant. He gave Isaac full assurance through the promise and made him the father of two peoples; and having made a promise to Jacob, he showed him Joseph. To the most faithful Moses he gave confidence in what was said through what befell Pharaoh; and having made a promise to David, he fulfilled it through Solomon, by which I mean the building of the temple. 8. But why do I need many words? There is nothing that God says which remains unfulfilled. Even if someone loses heart at once as he looks for the word to be fulfilled, the promise is still made good in time, and in time the promise is certainly fulfilled. For see: the things spoken long ago by the Lord and said many ages before, we now see fulfilled in the Gospels. Isaiah prophesied that Emmanuel would be born of a woman who had not known marriage; and he himself, born of Mary the Virgin and appearing as God, fulfilled the prophet's word. Micah foretold even the place where Christ was to be born; and the Lord himself, laid in a manger in Bethlehem, showed the prophet to be true. Zechariah announced to Jerusalem the good news of the Savior's entry; and the Lord himself, sending for the donkey and entering, fulfilled the prophecy in his own person. In short, so as not to name each of the things written, he himself became the fulfillment of the law and the prophets. What he had foretold through them, he himself accomplished when he came, fulfilling them and saying: “I who speak am here.” See, then, how now too the things proclaimed long ago about the Savior in the Psalms are fulfilled once again through the audacity of the soldiers. For what he had foretold that he would suffer, the crowds of the Jews now carry out, dividing the Savior's garments and giving him vinegar mixed with gall to drink. “For these things,” it says, “were done [?]

so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled”: the one that says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots”; and again, “They gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” 9. Many who read the Gospels and hear the phrase “so that what was written might be fulfilled” have supposed that the things that happened took place for no other reason than that the Scriptures might be fulfilled. From this they concluded that those who did them were not only blameless but even worthy of praise, because they acted not as sinners but as servants of what was written; for the words of the prophets would not have come true unless these people had done these deeds. They took this view especially because they were moved by the passages in John, where, in recounting the unbelief of the Jews, he says, in keeping with Isaiah's prophecy: “Though he had done so many signs before them, they did not believe, so that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke: Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” For if the Jews did not believe so that Isaiah's word might be fulfilled, then they were not responsible for their unbelief; rather, the one who said these things was, since it was because of him that they were fulfilled. “Take away the prophet's word,” they will say, “and they will certainly believe.” But such arguments and such an understanding fall far short of the truth. For neither is the prophet responsible for these things, nor are the Jews blameless for their own unbelief. The prophet foresaw what they were going to do and announced it; and they, doing it afterward, showed the prophet's word to be true. They did not dare to act against the Savior as servants of the prophetic words, but did these things willingly, by their own choice. So it was not the prophet who was the cause of their deeds, but their own will; rather, they were the cause of the prophet's saying these things about them. For it is the property of a prophet to see the future and not be mistaken, but each person's own will is the cause of his deeds. When we see things before our eyes, we are not deceived in seeing them, nor do we see them one way while they happen another way; as they happen, so we see them, and as we see them, so they happen. In the same way the prophets saw future things as present, and what they saw had to happen [?], and they had to see these things as certainly happening. And again, what we see with our eyes must necessarily exist, for we see the things that are, and they cannot happen otherwise than as we see them. In the same way, what the prophets foresaw had necessarily to be, and could not happen otherwise than as they had foreseen it. [?]

For if they did not foresee what was going to happen, they would no longer be prophets. And in general one must understand this: the prophets are not teachers of laws, whose only purpose is that what they command should be done. They foretell what is to come. Things do not happen because the prophets speak of them. The prophets foretell them because they are going to happen, and so the prophets cannot be wrong, for they truly see. Suppose, for argument's sake, that the prophets had not foretold it: it would still have been the Jews' own choice to do these things. In short, the saints do not compel what happens. They foresee the choice of those who act and make it known. Those who tried to refute this used to say, "Take away the prophet's word, and the Jews will certainly believe." In the same way I would say, "Take away the deeds of the Jews, and Isaiah would certainly not have prophesied such things about them." 19. So if John says, "The Jews did not believe in him, so that the word of Isaiah might be fulfilled," do not blame the prophet's word for their unbelief. Blame the conduct of the Jews themselves. What they were now doing, the prophet had foreseen long before. He could not be proved false. It had to be known that he had truly foreseen what is now happening. So that his word might be shown to be true to those who came after, the Jews were exposed as unbelievers who hid their unbelief. They were [?] wicked by their own choice, but since they kept their unbelief hidden, the word became their exposure. Was it not, then, because the word exposed them as they hid that they did not believe? And again, if he says, "The Jews could not believe, because what is against them is written," do not put this impossibility down to the will of those who acted, for they could have changed. The impossibility was that the prophet should lie. Since he had truly seen, he could not be mistaken. He saw it no otherwise than as it happened, and they were shown to be unbelievers. In the same way the miracle of the Virgin has been fulfilled, what concerned John has come to pass today, and everything written beforehand has been fulfilled. These things did not come about because they were written. They were foretold because they were certainly going to happen. So too the dividing of the garments has now taken place. It happened just as it was foreseen, and it was fulfilled and carried out just as it had been signified and announced beforehand. It is written thus: "When they had crucified him, they divided his garments by casting lots, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots." Matthew and the other evangelists simply say that the garments were divided, but John also describes the (Textual notes: Regius reads "if what happens"; Anglicanus, "if what has happened"; "so that not only"; then Anglicanus, "signifiers". [?])

manner of the division and the reason for casting the lot, in these words: "So the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, one part for each soldier. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top, so they said to one another, 'Let us [not?] tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be,' so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast

11. Perhaps someone who hears these things blushes. Perhaps someone who sees the Lord mocked, led away and beaten is ashamed. Perhaps someone who now sees the Lord, the Savior and King of all, judged by Pilate and crucified by the Jews is abashed and keeps his eyes on the ground. Not even the sun could bear to look on the sight. It was entirely darkened, so that it might turn away the eyes of others as well. It no longer heeded its command to shine for people, and in the end it even dared to disobey, when it saw the Master who had commanded it suffering at human hands. But if we learn the reason and see why he suffered, we no longer blush. Instead we marvel at his goodness and his love for humankind, and like Paul we too shall boast in the cross. For the Lord did not suffer for his own sake. It was we who were suffering in him. Human sin was great. This evil had already taken hold of the whole world. It was great even before this, and it grew little by little until it became unbearable for humankind. Death too had power to reign over all and against all. But our Lord is immortal and incorruptible, and just as he is immortal and incorruptible, so he is good and loves humankind. The Word of a good Father is good. So he did not let what he had made perish, and he would not allow anyone else to become lord of his works. He saw that wickedness was unbearable. He saw that the mortal race could not withstand death or pay the penalty for its evils, for the excess of wickedness was beyond every penalty. He saw also the goodness of the Father, and he saw his own sufficiency and power, for "Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God." Moved by his love for humankind and pitying our weakness, he put it on. For, as the prophet says, he himself took up our weaknesses, and our diseases (Textual note: others read "the eyes of others".)

he bore. Having pity on our mortality, he clothed himself with it. As Paul says, "He humbled himself to the point of death, even death on a cross." Seeing also that we were unable to pay the penalty, he took it on himself: "For Christ became a curse for us." So, having put on and clothed himself in what is human, he brought what is ours to the Father through himself. By suffering himself, he would make man unharmed in his suffering, and he would exchange small things for great. He came down to prepare our way up. He experienced birth so that through him we might become friends of the Unbegotten. He became weak for our sake so that we might be raised in power and say with Paul, "I can do all things in Jesus Christ who strengthens me." He took a corruptible body so that the corruptible might put on incorruption. He put on what is mortal so that the mortal might put on immortality. Finally he became man and died, so that we, who die as human beings, might be made divine and no longer have death reigning over us. For death has no dominion over us, as the apostolic word proclaims. This is why he is crucified: to buy back the curse, so that we might inherit the blessing. In his suffering he was not harmed at all. Instead he bestowed grace. In dying he did not remain dead, but gave life to the dead as well. And when he was slaughtered he did not perish. By the blood of his slaughter he redeemed absolutely everyone, while he himself remained beyond suffering. 19. If anyone asks how this happened, let him listen. In him two realities came together. I mean realities that are not equal and cannot be compared in any respect. The mortal was joined to the immortal, and a corruptible body was united with the incorruptible Word. The mortal did not harm the immortal, which was beyond suffering. Rather, under the mastery of death, the mortal itself remained beyond suffering, for what masters always rules over what is mastered. Because of the immortal Word who was united with it, death too was wondrously wiped out in it, as stubble is consumed by fire. The Word, being incorruptible, instead benefits the corruptible by being joined to it. Darkness is lit up by light, and the lesser is blessed by the greater. This is why the executioners now strip him of the garments we put on in Adam, the tunics of skin, so that in their place we may be able to put on Christ. This is why he also lets his garments be divided, so that we may have the Word who is undivided from the Father. "For I and the Father [?]

he says, "are one." This is why they also cast lots for the tunic, and why he endures this and lets it pass, so that Christ may become our lot, as the psalmist also says: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup." So he suffers nowhere else. He is crucified in no other place but the Place of the Skull, which the teachers of the Hebrews say is the tomb of Adam. They affirm that Adam was buried there after the curse. If this is so, I marvel at how fitting the place is. It was right that the Lord, who wished to renew the first Adam, should suffer in that very place, so that by releasing Adam from his sin he might take it away from the whole human race. Adam had heard, "Earth you are, and to earth you shall go." That is why the Lord in turn is laid there: so that, finding Adam there, he might lift the curse (margin: "Earth you are, and") and, instead of "Earth you are, and to earth you shall go," say at last: "Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you," and again: "Rise, come, follow me," so that you may no longer lie in the earth but go up to heaven. When the Savior is raised, Adam and all who are descended from Adam must be raised with him. Just as we too remained dead because of Adam when he died, so when the Lord's body is raised, all must be raised with it. This is what Paul means. He writes to the Corinthians, "For as in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive." 15. To see how they lead him to the cross, we must look at what is written. These things are certainly not without profit, and they were not written in the Gospels for nothing. After the Lord was judged... For he was judged and stood before the governor. Let no one be ashamed of this. He endured this too for our sake. Had he been ambushed in secret, the plot of the Jews might have stayed hidden. Through a trial, the false accusation of the plotters was brought into the open. If the Savior had not been tried, the Jews' envy of him would have remained hidden and merely suspected. Since he was tried, it could no longer escape anyone's notice. Pilate himself bore witness to the Savior's innocence and purity and brought the plot of the Jews to light. "For he knew," Scripture says, "that they had handed him over out of envy." Pilate would not have recognized the Jews' envy if the Savior had not stood trial. The Savior did something truly great and wonderful. By his silence he was at work, and by offering no defense he made the judge confess the (Textual note: Felckmann 2 reads γενομένους, ἐξένομεν [?].)

conspiracy, and admit that he had been swayed by the crowds rather than by justice. Had the Savior defended himself, one might have suspected that he feared death. Since he kept silent, one could only admire his firmness and courage. And for Pilate to make his own excuses in this way was nothing other than believing that the man on trial was God. Indeed, while he was being tried by Pilate, he sent a message to Pilate's wife, so that Pilate would be struck by his courage in silence and learn from the message that he was judging not a man but God. So the judge feared the one he judged. He was judged by his fear of the accused far more than he, as judge, struck any fear into the Lord. So he washed his hands, saying, "I am innocent of the blood of this man." Later, though, moved by his friendship with the Jews, he went along with their plotting and even handed him over to the cross. So the Savior is handed over, and once handed over he did not cower before death. Instead he stripped for the fight against it and pursued the fleeing serpent. The Lord was not like one who dies, but like one [?] death, for to this [?]. Then the wretched devil saw the wonder that had happened with Pilate: the judge cowered rather than the one being judged. He also saw the Lord now stripping for the fight against him. So he eagerly tried everything, wanting to learn what he had failed to learn when he tempted him on the mountain: whether this was the Son of God. Put to shame then, he waited for the time of death, thinking that he could test him in death too, since death was how he had enslaved everyone. For it is written in Luke that when the devil had finished every temptation, he left him until an opportune time. This is that time. The enemy himself knew that if he failed in this too, he would be trampled underfoot by all. Stripped of everything else, this was the only contest left to him. So he does everything to learn [?] whether this is the Savior. He did this so that, if he really learned the truth about him, he would not even dare to approach, knowing that his divine power is unapproachable. But the Lord saw his cunning. He saw that the devil was pursuing this not out of any reverence for him but in order to enslave humankind and tyrannize over all. So he hid his divinity and lived as a man. He did not want the devil to keep away from him as God and so escape unharmed. He wanted the devil to despise him as a man and approach him, and from then on begin to be mocked by men. Picture someone who sees his opponent cowering and therefore running away, and who pretends to be weak (Textual note: [?] the editions, however, read κατέπληξεν.)

to draw him on. The one who was fleeing, seeing the pretended weakness, takes courage and comes close, and the noble wrestler, who drew him on by weakness, defeats him by his own strength. In the same way the Lord drew the enemy on by human weakness, and by his own power he strengthened man against the enemy. That is why, at the time of his death, he is distressed and begins to be deeply sorrowful. He prayed that that cup might pass, and he cried out, "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak," so that our adversary, approaching him as a man, might come up against divine power. 15. Drawn on by these things, the wretch was made a fool of and approached the Lord. Then, seeing his courage, he cowered. But seeing also the weakness of the body, he grew bold again. From then on one could see the devil fleeing with his whole army, his principalities and powers, and the Lord pursuing the devil's battle line with human weapons. Little time passed before he had stripped the enemy of everything. Put to shame, the enemy then took matters into his own hands and stirred up everything against the Lord. He stirred up the Jews to conspire, Pilate to condemn, and the soldiers to mock him. But he did not know that he was doing this against himself. Wickedness is blind and evil has no foresight. It did not know that it was sharpening its hands against itself. Think of someone who grabs a snake by the [?], meaning to throw it at another: he is certainly bitten himself. Or think of someone who holds fire in his hand, meaning to harm his enemy: he does not know that he will certainly be burned himself. In the same way, wickedness wages war on those who use it, and it harms those who hold it more than those they want to send it against. So Pharaoh, wanting to overtake, was overtaken; having begun to pursue, he was pursued; and wanting to kill, he was drowned. So Goliath was cut down by the very things in which he took pride, and wanting to plunder, he was plundered. The wretched devil suffered in the same way. Wanting to tempt, he was tempted. He stirred up the soldiers, or rather he himself was stirred up in the executioners, and he worked everything against himself. He had only just been stripped of his spoils, and the victory was hidden from people's sight. But the wretch himself brought it into the open, though against his will. For when the Lord had stripped for the fight and the trophy over the devil had been won unseen, then, so that this too might become manifest, they at once clothed him, as John (Textual notes: (89) "strengthened by his own power": Felckmann 5; omitted in Regius and Felckmann 5 [?]. (90) [?] reads "at the very time of death". (91) At the word "flesh" [?] Felckmann 5.)

[?] a sign of great [?]. For the one they had judged as a man, they now worshipped as God as he died. The one they despised as worthless, they confessed as king. The one whose ordinary garments they took away, they dressed in purple. The one they insulted without knowing him, they called a prophet, even against their will. The one they mocked as they struck him, they presented with the prizes of victory: the scarlet cloak, the crown of thorns and the reed. They did these things as insults, but they did not know that, even against their will, they were being stripped by him. Through sin the devil had made the earth a place of murder, and it was soaked with blood more than with water. At the beginning it had opened its mouth and received the blood of righteous Abel, and afterwards people went on mingling blood with blood, as it is written: "Cursing and lying and theft and adultery are poured out over the earth, and they mingle blood with blood." That is why the earth was also cursed, as God said: "And now cursed is the earth, which opened its mouth to receive the blood of your brother Abel." Even before that, the Master had cursed it because of Adam's transgression, saying: "Cursed is the earth in your labors; in sorrow you shall eat of it all the days of your life." Everything was full of blood, and thorns sprang up everywhere because of the curse. Holding the written bond of all this, the enemy exalted himself over all and ruled as a tyrant, since he had everyone in his power. For this reason the Lord stripped him of all these things, and then, as he was led to his death, he wore them. He did this to show what his death accomplished: that it did not happen for nothing but for our salvation. The blood he wore in the scarlet cloak, the thorns in the crown, and the written bond in the reed, with which the devil had long been writing against us. He did this so that along with death he might at last wipe these things out too and cleanse creation of them. In place of the thorns he would give the tree of life. In place of the blood of sin he would cleanse the earth and everyone with his own blood. And in place of the curse he would at last bless those on earth, saying: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth." This is why, bearing our blood, he poured out his own upon the earth. From it, in place of thorns, good things and life have sprung up in it. Looking to this, holy David says: "I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living." 17. There is another reason why he wore the crown of thorns: to wipe out the cares of our life. Without meaning to, the wretch cast our cares upon him. He did not know that the Lord, by bearing them,

would make everyone free of care against him, so that the seed of the word would be free of thorns and our prayers free of distraction. He himself suffered pain and anxiety for us so that we might be free of pain. This is also why the Lord took the reed from them. The devil himself handed it to the Lord, not knowing that he was sharpening the sword against himself. For the reed is said to be deadly to snakes, and they are struck down by it more than by anything else. Since the Lord of Hosts himself, as Isaiah says, was pursuing the fleeing dragon, the serpent, the great devil, the Lord took from them the thing that destroys him. In this way the devil would be weakened by his own weapons, and humankind strengthened by the Lord's. David did something like this with Goliath, when he took the enemy's sword and cut off the enemy's head with it. The Savior has now done the same by taking the reed from them. He did so not only to free us from the serpent's deceit, but also to kill the serpent itself with the reed and show it to be dead. So the wretch was made a fool of in this way. He saw himself fallen from the very things in which he had exalted himself against us. He saw himself cast out of the earth, and the earth cleansed of blood and thorns. He saw that he had lost the written bond and the reed with which he wrote against us. Yet once again he dares what should never be dared, and strikes himself all the harder by it. For the evil one heard the Lord say, "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." He thought that the Word shared the weakness of the body, and not rather that the body was strengthened by the power of the Word. So again he attempts lawless things. He provokes the executioners against the Savior, while he himself clung to the thorns and rolled about in them, and suffered the very opposite of what he intended. While he had them, he lost them, and he thought that he could take them when he did not have them. But he did not take them until the Savior had lifted the curse against us that lay in them. Once the Lord had borne the curse, the devil took back the thorns and the cloak. They no longer had power against us, but they exposed the wickedness of those men. For now the devil himself is in the thorns, as though kicking against the goads in his attack on us. And concerning the scarlet cloak it is said to him: just as a garment soaked in blood is not

…the devil who had stirred them up, striking at him among the thorns. And just as the nations that went up against Jerusalem struck one another down in the valley of Jehoshaphat, and as those pursuing Israel, when they came to the shore, became entangled with one another and seized hold of one another, so now too those persecuting the Lord were striking one another without knowing it. They did him no harm at all, but rather wronged themselves. For if someone wanted to strike a rock with his hand, he would not cut the rock but would wound his hand. In the same way, those acting against the Lord dared to attack the incorruptible and were themselves corrupted, and set their hands against the immortal and rather died themselves. And the worst of it was that he suffered through his own members, and this, above all, brought the villain to utter shame. Had he been struck by the Lord at all, he could have boasted of it; but when he is struck by those who served him, this surpassed all shame. Yet it is not their blow that destroys the serpent, for they could not do so much, being men, and executioners at that. The outrage the Jews inflicted on him grieved him, but what wounded him was not the blow they struck. It was the Lord, who struck back against their blow, and the power that passed from the Saviour's hand into the reed. For in this too the Lord took on a guise and put forward what is human. He received the serpent among the thorns, and, being struck as a man, he allowed the executioners to strike the serpent. So the one who once boasted that he was God, and boasted that he had put the Lord to the test, was struck by executioners and carried off complete shame.

19. These things turned out for him contrary to what he intended. Working in those who cried out against the Saviour, he did not realize that he was bringing silence to bear against himself. In provoking Pilate, he did not know that he was producing fearlessness instead of cowardice. In stirring up the beating of the Lord, he was mistaken, for it put forbearance on display. And finally, in his drunken outrage against the Saviour, he did not see that he was arming virtue against vice. For the enemy delights in every vice and wickedness, and whatever is evil is the devil's weapon: he persuades people to sin either through fear of death or through the urge to retaliate at all costs. That is why the Lord endured everything. He meant to teach that courage stands against cowardice, forbearance against insult, gentleness against anger, and in all things virtue against vice. First he taught us to turn the other cheek to the one who strikes; and, 'Do not fear those who kill the body'; and, 'Do not demand back what is yours from one who takes it'; and, 'Bless those who persecute you.' But so that some would not think the commandment impossible, for this reason [textual note (6), partly illegible: […] 'he suffered through his own members.']

the Lord demonstrated everything in his own person. By what he suffered he persuaded everyone not to insult in return when insulted, not to strike back when struck, not to grow angry when mocked, not to demand back what is ours from one who takes it, and in general not to fear death but even to despise it in the hope of what is to come. For in this way victory over the devil and over every sin comes more easily than when we retaliate. When we retaliate, wronging in return those who wrong us and insulting those who insult us, we increase and feed the vice against ourselves. We wrong ourselves more than our enemies, because of the condemnation that vice brings and the judgment that awaits those who practise it. But when, like the Lord, we endure being wronged, and set forbearance against those who revile us, courage against those who threaten us, and the hope of immortality against death, we certainly grieve the enemy by these things. He falls before that full armour with which Paul too arms us, when he says: 'Put on, then, the whole armour of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil.' For so too, when the Saviour endured, these words came true: 'I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning.'

20. Immediately, then, after the Lord had borne himself valiantly in these things and the enemy had fallen, they laid the cross on him. Without meaning to, they were truly supplying a token of victory against themselves. As long as the enemy stood, the executioners held the wood; but once he had fallen and been dashed down, the Lord took up the trophy and carried it himself. For the victor, triumphing over the devil, had to carry the trophy himself and not leave it to another. Along with the trophy he also received his garments back from them as he went off to death, so that he might strip these off together with death. For this reason, ready to be stripped again, he urged on those who were leading him away. As he was led away, according to John he carried the cross himself, but according to the other evangelists, Simon, a man of Cyrene, carried the cross. This does not contradict John, nor does John write anything contrary to the others: both things happened here. The Lord carried the cross himself, and Simon in turn carried it. He carried it as a trophy against the devil [?], and he bore the cross himself willingly, for he did not go to his death under compulsion. And Simon in turn carried it so that all might know that it was not his own death but that of men [?]

[?] the Lord dies. When this had happened, he came hurrying to the place where he had to mount the cross. There he would nail to the cross the bond written against us, which [?] from the enemies; and, having stripped the principalities and powers, he would make a public show of them, triumphing over them on the wood. There he would show the man snatched from the lion, and would sprinkle and cleanse the earth with his own blood [?]. As he was about to do this, he took off his garments. For in bringing man into paradise, he had to strip off the tunics that Adam received when he was driven out of paradise. When Adam sinned and was from then on destined to die, he received tunics of skin, made from dead animals, a symbol of the deadness that had come upon him through sin.

21. But the Lord, who took up all that is ours for our sake, put these on so that he might also strip them off, and clothe us instead with life and incorruption. Together with these he also put on a seamless tunic, woven from the top in one piece throughout. Even from these the Jews might have been able to believe who the wearer of these garments was and where he came from: that the Word was not from the earth but had come from above; that the Word of the Father is not divided but indivisible; and that when he became man, he did not have a body stitched together from a man and a woman, but woven from the Virgin alone by the art of the Spirit. So the executioners divide his other garments, since they can be divided, and they are divided into four. For he wore these for the sin of the fourfold world, east and west and north and south. Seeing him clothed in them, John said: 'Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.' The tunic alone they did not dare to tear, out of fear of the sign it made known. This too was not their doing but the work of the one hanging there. For as he hung there as a man, he was pursuing the principalities, overpowering the devil, and frightening the executioners so that they would not tear the tunic. As long as it remained whole, the reproof against the Jews would remain too, a reproof that came shortly afterwards: the veil was torn, but the Saviour's tunic was not divided by the executioners and stayed whole. For the Gospel stays whole for ever, while the shadows are divided. Now when he had stripped off his garments for death, the devil in turn saw the Saviour's eagerness. He saw himself fallen from heaven and cast out of the earth, and he did not know what to do, for everything around him was full of turmoil and perplexity. He could not stay, yet he was afraid to flee. Then he reflected that those who die must die on the earth, as it is written: 'Earth you are, and to earth you shall return.' Afraid to remain on earth and be caught there, from then on he [?]

flew up into the air, hoping perhaps that in this way, once the Lord's body was laid on the earth, he might have the air to himself. But the Lord, showing his love for humanity in this too, did not die on the earth. He went up into the air by means of the cross, pursuing the serpent there too, so that he might drive the ruler of the power of the air out of that place as well and cast down the spiritual forces of wickedness. Yet he did not leave the earth untended either. For as he hung on the cross, he cleansed the air by stretching out his hands, and he redeemed the earth, washing it clean with the blood and water from his side.

22. What, then, was the enemy to do after suffering all this? He had fallen from heaven, been cast out of the earth, and been chased from the air. On top of this, he was ashamed at having promised great things and accomplished nothing. Beaten on every side and at a loss on every side, he decided at least to guard Hades, for that place was still left to him. He feared that the Lord would come down there, drive him out, and set free all who were under his power. So he stirred up and threw everything into confusion, calling on everyone for help. Once more he provoked the Jews to reproach the Lord, to insult him and laugh at him without restraint. Whatever was left of his armour, he hurled it all against the Lord, hoping perhaps in this way to get hold of him as one answerable for sin. The Jews mocked the Lord, saying: 'If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.' But the Saviour, who truly is the Son of God, wanted to be known as Son of God not by fleeing death but by remaining, and by remaining to trample death down, and so to be known as life itself. He could indeed have come down from the cross, he who had raised others from the dead. But coming down would have shown a flight from death, whereas staying made known nothing other than that the one who stayed was life. That is why the devil was so intent on having the Lord reproached in these things. He wanted him to come down from the cross and not to be among the dead, so that he himself might at least get away unscathed and stay master of the dead. For he feared that, as it is written, he would go up to the height of the cross, lead captivity captive, and receive gifts among men; he suspected that this might be the one about whom these things are written. So the villain stirred up the Pharisees again, and even made them promise, beyond all measure, to believe, if only he would come down from the cross. He set everything in motion and made promises against his own will, only so that the Lord would not become dead and go down into Hades. So again he made the Pharisees say: 'He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him.' But the dragon, the teacher of unbelief, did not want the Pharisees to believe. What he wanted was

23. That, then, was why they reproached him: so that salvation would not come to others. For the meddler knew that the Lord was not simply dying, but that his death would become salvation and life for all. That is why he wanted him to come down from the cross, and made the Pharisees promise to believe, hoping perhaps that through the promise of faith he might get what he wanted. But the Lord, who is truly the Saviour and seeks not his own interest but ours, wanted to be known as Saviour not by saving himself but by redeeming creation. A physician will not be known as a physician from his own good health, unless he also shows his skill on the sick. And the sun, if it draws its rays in upon itself, will not be known as light, unless it also stretches them out over the world and [dispels] the darkness with them. So too the Lord did not save himself, for he had no need of salvation, being himself the Saviour. He wanted to be known to all as Saviour through the good he did for others. Nor did he want to be known as Son of God by coming down from the cross, but by remaining on it. For the Saviour's death brings people far more faith and salvation than his coming down from the cross would have done. Indeed, while he was still hanging on the cross, the tombs were opened and those lying in them were saved, and the thief hanging beside him believed in him. This showed that he is truly the Saviour, and that even in dying he bears fruit through faith. At this the devil was at last truly astounded, and was gripped, as he deserved, by utter perplexity. He saw that he had lost even the thief on the cross. The man he had long ago persuaded to rob, he now saw believing; the man he had provoked to blaspheme, he now saw worshipping the Lord and rebuking the other thief, or rather the devil in that thief. And he was tormented once more, because he saw the man he had put to death as a thief being carried over into paradise.

24. He saw too that all his armour had been thrown down, and that there was no defence he had sent out that the Lord had not made useless, as it is written: 'The swords of the enemy have failed utterly, and you have destroyed cities.' So he was troubled, and in his perplexity he tried, as a last resort, giving the Saviour vinegar mixed with gall to drink. But here too he did not realize that he was contriving against himself. For he was handing over to the Saviour the bitterness of wrath, which had arisen through the transgression of the law and in which he held everyone captive. And the Saviour received it, consumed it and drained it, so that instead of the vinegar

he might give us to drink the wine that Wisdom mixed; instead of the gall, he might bestow on us words sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; and in return for his tasting what is ours, he might say to us as well: 'Taste and see that the Lord is good.' When the devil had failed in this too and been despoiled, he was at last put to shame. Seeing such great things, he began to suspect that he was fighting not against a man but against God. For he saw that the very means by which he used to hunt everyone were now bringing him to shame, and that he was falling rather than throwing down. So he tried to withdraw and turn his back in flight. Seeing the Lord hanging there and pursuing death, he feared that this was the one of whom it is written: 'The Lord will be exalted to have mercy on us.' For this reason he sought all the more to abandon everything and flee, begrudging those who would receive mercy from the Lord. But the Lord, who is truly the Saviour, did not want him to get away unharmed, nor to leave his work unfinished, nor to abandon to the enemy those held captive in Hades. So he devised a great and marvellous stratagem. Seeing the bold one cowering, trembling and afraid, he again took on the appearance of one giving way, so that the enemy would come close and he could subdue him completely. For the dragon did not want the Lord to die, nor even to hang on the wood. He wanted the Lord to come down from the cross and not die; or, if he would not come down, then at least simply to stay on the wood, provided only that he did not die. For he feared that what is written might come to pass: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind.' And so he feared that this was the one anointed and sent, and that freedom would then come for all.

25. Stripped of everything, then, he prayed that he might at least keep hold of Hades. For again he feared that this was the one who lights up even the darkness, of whom it is written: 'Galilee of the nations, the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light.' And he had heard him say: 'I am the light.' So he was afraid that the Lord would die and that he himself would be cast out of everything. But the Lord saw him fleeing. So that this would not happen and the enemy would not escape as a fugitive, he uttered human cries, cries of weakness, saying: 'Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?', that is, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' He did this so that the devil, who had been terrified of him as God, would take him for a weak man and not escape as a fugitive. Lured by these cries, the all-wicked one came at him again as at a man, and was dashed to pieces. For he persuaded the Jews to demand that he be slain, and something happened that he had not foreseen. The Lord was pierced not in any other part but in the side, from which flowed water and blood. Since deception had first come through the woman formed from a side, so through the side of the second Adam there might be a ransom and a cleansing for the former [deception]

— a ransom through the blood, and a cleansing through the water. This did not turn out as the devil intended. The very death he feared would happen was the death the Lord died, and the devil was despoiled. Thinking he would hold Christ fast in death, he was himself shown to be the one who was dead; and boasting that he was setting a trap for a man, he caused him to be known as God. For as soon as he died, creation was left without the sun, the veil of the temple was torn, the earth quaked and the rocks were split, and the soldiers cowered, together with the gatekeepers of Hades. From all this one could see that he was no longer a mere man but truly God in a body, as those watching said: 'Truly this is the Son of God.' For many tombs were opened, and their dead were raised.

26. Vice is truly blind. Thinking it was killing one, it has been robbed of all; and thinking it was bringing him down to Hades, it has itself been cast out of Hades. And it was shown to all that the Saviour did not die through weakness of nature. He pursued death in order to destroy it, so that he might abolish it and set free those who through fear of death had been subject to slavery all their lives. Not long afterwards, then, he went forth [?] and loosed the pangs of Hades, and he raised the others, saying: 'Rise, let us go from here.' He himself rose again and returned to life from death, treating its daring as a joke. This was foretold in the hymns, where the Spirit says: 'He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will scoff at them.' For he is truly mocked, having been made a plaything in this way, since things turned out against his intent. Think of the little creature called the wasp: it attacks a rock and does it no harm by the attack, but rather loses its own sting. So too death went badly astray when it attacked Life, which is Christ. It could not hold him in death; instead it lost its sting as well. And so those whom its sting once terrified now jeer at it and say: 'Where, O Death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, is your victory?' And again: 'Death, having grown strong, swallowed up.' And again: 'God has wiped away every tear from every'

"When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted. Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with gladness."
